headline: If the repair touched any of these, plan on a calibration.
body:
If the repair touched any of these, plan on a calibration.

Windshield. Front bumper cover, grille, emblem or bumper beam. Rear bumper cover, quarter panel or rear body. A side mirror with a camera in it. A liftgate or tailgate with a camera. A wheel alignment, struts, springs, tires a different size, a lift. An airbag deployment. Any ADAS sensor, camera or bracket, for any reason.

Write the line on the estimate now. It is cheaper than the tow that brings the car back.

headline: Subaru with EyeSight: any collision repair gets a calibration.
body:
Subaru with EyeSight. Any collision repair gets the EyeSight calibration. Not just glass.

A hit anywhere on the car can tilt the body a fraction of a degree, and the stereo camera sees it. Subaru bulletin 18-231-23 has us check body angle with a digital gauge before the cal.

Write it on every Subaru collision RO. Spec OE glass and save yourself the second trip.

headline: On the windshield, behind the mirror.
body:
Sensor 1 of 9. The forward camera.

It sits on the windshield behind the mirror and runs lane keep, auto brake and adaptive cruise. Every glass R&R moves it. Roof and A-pillar work moves it. An alignment changes where it looks.

Ask your cal shop: is this OE glass, and does the shop know it is a camera car?

body:
Sensor 2 of 9. The front radar.

It hides behind the emblem or grille and rides on the bumper beam. Pull the grille, refinish the cover, replace the beam, and the radar moved. On a Toyota it will not set a code when it is a little off. Clean scan, wrong radar.

Front hit means radar calibration. Every time.

body:

Ask your cal shop: was the front camera calibrated with the radar after the grille went back on?

headline: Usually verify. Rarely calibrate.
body:
Sensor 4 of 9. Front park sensors.

They live in the bumper cover. Most makes want them verified, not calibrated. What breaks them is paint, plastic weld and the wrong cover. Ford lists the sensor retainer rings as no-repair parts.

Ask your cal shop: were the park sensors verified on the post-scan?

headline: Two radars, one each corner.
body:
Sensor 6 of 9. Blind spot radars.

One each corner behind the rear bumper cover, bracketed to the quarter panel. Rear cross traffic uses the same two. Rear cover R&R, quarter repair, rear body work, all move them. Refinish counts.

On Toyota, Honda, Acura, Hyundai and Kia the module bolts to the quarter, not the cover, and we usually have to adjust it by hand. We calibrate those with the cover off.

Ask your cal shop: can you come before the rear cover goes back on?

headline: Move the wheels, move the aim.
body:
Sensor 9 of 9. Wheels and suspension.

Thrust angle decides where the forward camera and the front radar look. Alignment, struts, springs, control arms, tie rods, tires a different size, a lift. All of it moves the aim. Most makes require a recalibration after an alignment, plus a steering angle sensor reset.

Ask your cal shop: alignment first, then calibration, and was the SAS reset?

headline: Hard enough to fire the bags is hard enough to move structure.
body:
Red flag on the RO: airbag deployment.

The hit was hard enough to fire the bags, so it was hard enough to move the structure the camera and radar bolt to. Treat the front systems as suspect even when the parts look fine. If seats or pretensioners were replaced, check the OEM for an occupant sensor zero-point too.

Ask your cal shop: was the front structure measured, and were camera and radar calibrated after the pull?

headline: No code does not mean calibrated.
body:
No code does not mean calibrated.

A scan finds what is broken. It does not prove the aim is right. Those are two different questions and the scan tool only answers one.

Ford put it in writing on May 1, 2026. Calibration is required for all vehicles with ADAS-related repairs, regardless of whether a DTC is present. Pre-scan before the estimate is final. Repair. Calibrate. Post-scan before delivery.

"Scanned, no codes found" is not a calibration.

headline: Why the type of calibration matters to your schedule.
body:
Bay or road. Why it matters to your delivery promise.

Bay means targets on a level floor with no metal in the radar's view. We do it at your shop, same day. Road means a drive at speed on a road with good lane lines, in daylight, usually not in rain.

GM and Jeep cameras calibrate on the road. Toyota, Subaru and VW in the bay. Honda and Nissan need both, bay first. Tesla teaches itself over miles, and Autopilot says unavailable until it is done.

Plan the road time before you promise the car.

headline: Six things, or it is not done.
body:
Six things on the calibration paperwork, or it is not done.

1. The OEM procedure by name. 2. Pre-scan and post-scan reports. 3. Target setup or aim values, before and after. 4. Bay, road or both. 5. VIN, tech, date. 6. Any fault found and what was done about it.

That paperwork is what gets the line paid. It is also what keeps your shop's name off a subrogation letter six months from now.

kicker: WHEN YOU DO NOT NEED ONE
headline: Usually no.
body:
Three things that usually do not need a calibration.

A mirror with only a blind spot light in it. A door skin or door shell alone. A battery disconnect with no parts touched.

Verify them on the post-scan and move on. One exception worth knowing: some GM front cameras need a relearn after a dead battery.

We tell you when the answer is no. That is how you know the yes means something.

headline: Clean scan, wrong radar.
body:
Toyota and Lexus.

The radar sits behind the emblem and will not throw a code when it is a little off. Clean scan, wrong radar. Front hit means radar calibration, every time, and the emblem has to be the radar version.

Rear hit: the blind spot modules bolt to the quarter panel and usually need a hand adjustment. We calibrate them with the rear cover off. Call before the cover goes back on.

The RAV4 is the car we calibrate most. The guide is drawn on one.

headline: Bay first, then the road.
body:
Honda and Acura.

The forward camera aims in the bay and then on the road, in that order. LaneWatch and 360 cameras in the mirror need aiming after a mirror R&R. Honda calls for camera aiming after an alignment on many models. The blind spot radars mount to the quarter panel, so we calibrate them with the rear cover off.

Ask your cal shop: did the static come before the drive, and did they want the rear cover off?

If the adjuster pushes back on a Ford, the position statement does the talking.

GM.

The forward camera calibrates on the road. It needs miles, lane lines and daylight, so build the drive into the delivery promise. Digital surround-view cameras need no cal. Analog ones do. A dead battery can knock a front camera into relearn.

Tell us the day before and the drive is done before your customer shows up.

headline: You do not get a code in the bay.

Ask your cal shop: how many coats over the radar?

kicker: MAKES WE SEE EVERY WEEK · HYUNDAI, KIA, GENESIS
headline: Check the bracket before the drive.
body:
Hyundai, Kia, Genesis.

The rear corner radars mount to the quarter panel and most need a hand adjustment, so we calibrate them with the rear cover off. Then the drive self-aligns. A bracket bent two degrees still completes the routine and still reads wrong on the road. Check the bracket before the drive, not after the comeback.

Ask your cal shop: did you look at the bracket, and did you want the cover off?

headline: Camera on the road, radar in the bay.

Jeep, Ram, Chrysler.

Plan the bay time and the drive time, in that order.

kicker: HOW WE WORK WITH YOUR SHOP
headline: Every calibration we recommend, your shop gets paid for.
body:
Every calibration we recommend, your shop gets paid for.

If the carrier denies a calibration after our documentation, you do not pay us for it. We write the OEM-cited rebuttal and it usually flips on the next round. That is the deal, on every invoice.

And keep the math in mind. Most calibration lines cost less than the tow that brings the car back.
